CORS protects against CSRF attacks -> CORS does NOT protect against CSRF. In fact, misconfigured CORS can make CSRF easier.

Cross-origin authentication always requires CORS -> Cross-origin authentication can use multiple mechanisms, not just CORS. Authentication Methods: CORS with Credentials: JSONP (Legacy): PostMessage API: OAuth 2.0 Redirects:
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: is safe for APIs -> Using wildcard (``) is dangerous when credentials are involved and can expose sensitive data.

system-vs-personal-api-tokens.title: System vs Personal API Tokens
system-vs-personal-api-tokens.blurb: Programmatic access to APIs is almost always authenticated with bearer credentials: opaque tokens, JWTs, API keys, or OAuth access tokens. In product security interviews, "system vs personal" is shorthand for who the credential represents (a machine identity vs a human) and what breaks when that identity rotates
mustKnow: ✅ Secure storage (secret management for system tokens)
traps: Personal tokens are less secure than system tokens -> Security depends on how tokens are managed, not just the type. Both can be secure or insecure depending on implementation.
System tokens should have all permissions for convenience -> System tokens should follow the principle of least privilege - only grant minimum necessary permissions.
Token rotation is only for personal tokens -> Both system and personal tokens should be rotated regularly, though rotation strategies may differ.
Token storage in environment variables is always secure -> Environment variables are one option but have limitations and aren't always the most secure approach.

iam-and-least-privilege-at-scale.title: IAM and Least Privilege at Scale
iam-and-least-privilege-at-scale.blurb: Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the discipline of ensuring the right subjects (humans, workloads, devices) can access the right resources, with the right permissions, for the right reasons, only when needed, with full auditability.
mustKnow: AWS: SCP guardrails, permission boundaries, IAM Access Analyzer findings as backlog
GCP: Custom roles, deny policies org-wide, service account keys discouraged
Azure: PIM for roles, managed identities, conditional access on admin tasks
traps: RBAC alone guarantees least privilege. -> Roles drift (new permissions creep in); you need reviews, policy-as-code tests, and JIT elevation where appropriate.
Temporary admin access is low risk. -> Without strict expiry, break-glass auditing, and session recording, temporary becomes permanent culture.
IAM cleanup is a one-time project. -> Joiner/mover/leaver events, new services, and emergency grants continuously reopen over-privilege.
Cloud IAM console defaults are fine. -> Wildcard ARNs, `` actions, and cross-account trusts are common audit findings-deny by default patterns help.

xss.title: XSS
xss.blurb: XSS lets attackers run JavaScript in victims' browsers in the origin of your app-stealing cookies where possible, performing actions, defacing UI, or pivoting to supply chain via admin sessions.
mustKnow: ✅ Output encoding (HTML, JavaScript, URL, CSS contexts)
traps: XSS only affects applications with user-generated content -> XSS can occur anywhere user input is reflected or stored, not just in user-generated content.
Input validation prevents XSS -> Input validation helps but does NOT prevent XSS. Only output encoding prevents XSS.
XSS only affects browsers - server-side code is safe -> XSS affects client-side rendering, but the vulnerability is in server-side code that doesn't properly encode output.

csrf.title: CSRF
csrf.blurb: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) is a security vulnerability that allows attackers to trick authenticated users into performing unwanted actions on a web application. It ranks in OWASP Top 10 and is a critical web application security risk.
mustKnow: ✅ CSRF tokens in all state-changing operations
✅ Never use GET for state-changing operations
traps: CSRF and XSS are the same thing -> CSRF and XSS are completely different attacks with different goals and mitigation strategies.
HTTPS prevents CSRF -> HTTPS does NOT prevent CSRF. HTTPS only encrypts the connection; it doesn't verify request origin.
Only POST requests can be CSRF vulnerable -> Any state-changing operation can be vulnerable, regardless of HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE).

CSRF tokens alone are sufficient -> CSRF tokens are the primary defense, but defense in depth is recommended. CSRF Token Implementation: Additional Defenses: SameSite cookies (Strict or Lax) Origin/Referer header

xss-vs-csrf.title: XSS vs CSRF
xss-vs-csrf.blurb: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) and CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) are two of the most common web application vulnerabilities. While both involve "cross-site" attacks, they are fundamentally different and require different mitigation strategies.
traps: XSS and CSRF are the same attack -> XSS and CSRF are completely different attacks with different goals, mechanisms, and mitigations.
Preventing XSS also prevents CSRF -> XSS and CSRF require different mitigation strategies. Preventing one does not prevent the other.

XSS can only be used to steal cookies -> XSS can be used for multiple attack vectors, not just cookie theft. XSS Attack Vectors: Cookie Theft: document.cookie Session Hijacking: Steal session tokens Keylogging: Capture
CSRF only affects GET requests -> CSRF can affect any state-changing request, including POST, PUT, DELETE, etc. GET Requests (Less Common): POST Requests (More Common):

cors-and-sop.title: CORS and SOP
cors-and-sop.blurb: An origin is defined by three components: Scheme (Protocol): http:// or https:// Host (Domain): example.com Port: 80 (HTTP) or 443 (HTTPS) - default ports are implicit.
mustKnow: CSRF attacks work by tricking browser
Use SameSite or CSRF tokens for CSRF protection
traps: CORS is a security feature that protects my server -> CORS is a relaxation of the Same-Origin Policy, not a security feature that protects your server.
CORS protects against CSRF attacks -> CORS does NOT protect against CSRF attacks. In fact, misconfigured CORS can make CSRF attacks easier.
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: is safe for public APIs -> Using wildcard () with credentials is dangerous and violates the CORS specification.
CORS Does NOT Protect Your Server -> CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server Direct requests (curl, Postman

browser-and-frontend-runtime-security-de.title: Browser and Frontend Runtime Security Deep Dive
browser-and-frontend-runtime-security-de.blurb: Modern browsers are not a single "trusted runtime." They combine origins, process isolation, content policies, and network metadata to contain compromise. After any cross-site scripting (XSS) or supply-chain incident, attacker-controlled JavaScript can still run in your page's origin.
mustKnow: CSP - default-src, nonces or hashes, frame-ancestors, restrict script-src
Cookie flags - HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite (pair with CSRF tokens / double submit where needed)
Subresource Integrity - on third-party script/link when not self-hosted
Fetch metadata / isolation - Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy, Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy where applicable
dangerouslySetInnerHTML · v-html · innerHTML assignment · document.write · URL handlers feeding javascript: / data: · unsanitized postMessage
Prefer HttpOnly session or BFF pattern; avoid long-lived secrets in localStorage/sessionStorage (XSS = game over).
traps: React/Vue/Svelte prevents XSS. -> Unsafe sinks (dangerouslySetInnerHTML, v-html, URL handlers), third-party scripts, and DOM API misuse reintroduce XSS.
We can add CSP later. -> Retrofit CSP without nonces/hashes often breaks ads/analytics; early design (no inline handlers, bundle discipline) cheapens rollout.
Subresource Integrity is optional for first-party JS. -> CDN compromise and build tampering justify SRI or first-party hosting with integrity checks on critical paths.
localStorage is fine for tokens if we minify. -> Any secret readable by JS is stealable via XSS-prefer HttpOnly cookies with CSRF defenses or BFF patterns.

security-headers.title: Security Headers
security-headers.blurb: HTTP Security Headers are response headers that instruct browsers to enforce security policies on behalf of the server. They form a browser-enforced defense-in-depth layer that mitigates entire classes of attacks-XSS, clickjacking, MIME confusion, protocol downgrade
mustKnow: Purpose: Prevents XSS attacks by controlling resource loading
Best Practice: Start with report-only mode, then enforce
Best Practice: Use preload for maximum security
Best Practice: Always set to nosniff
traps: CSP unsafe-inline is fine with HTTPS. -> TLS doesn't stop XSS; unsafe-inline weakens CSP's main value.
HSTS means attackers can't use HTTP. -> First visit and misconfigured subdomains still matter; preload lists help but aren't universal.
X-Frame-Options is obsolete-ignore it. -> Older clients and some embed scenarios still benefit; frame-ancestors in CSP is modern preference, not instant removal everywhere.
Referrer-Policy is a privacy-only header. -> It also reduces token leakage in Referer URLs.

open-redirect.title: Open Redirect
open-redirect.blurb: An open redirect occurs when an application sends the browser to a user-controlled URL (or builds a URL from untrusted parts) without strict validation.
mustKnow: User-controlled target → Location: or JS navigate → external site (CWE-601)
Phishing · OAuth code/token theft · chain to SSRF/malware
Parse URL · allowlist host (exact) or path-only /safe/path · reject // and \
//evil · subdomain trick · double encode · unicode host
redirect_uri exact match · no open wildcards
OAuth · SSRF · XSS · Web App Vulnerabilities
"Never reflect raw URLs into redirects-allowlist or internal paths only, parse and canonicalize."
traps: Open redirect is always Low severity. -> Phishing against high-value users or OAuth chains can be High/Critical.
Blocking http:// fixes it. -> Attacker can use https:// or scheme-relative //.
startswith('trusted.example') is enough. -> https://trusted.example.evil.com and encoding tricks bypass naive prefix checks.
Client-side redirect validation is sufficient. -> Attacker calls server directly with malicious parameter-validate server-side.

web-cache-poisoning-and-deception.title: Web Cache Poisoning and Deception
web-cache-poisoning-and-deception.blurb: Web cache poisoning tricks a shared cache (CDN, reverse proxy, browser) into storing a malicious response keyed incorrectly, so other users receive attacker-controlled content. Web cache deception tricks a cache into storing private data at a URL that looks static or public, enabling unauthorized retrieval.
mustKnow: Poisoning Store bad representation under victim-shared key
Deception Store private data where unauthenticated clients hit
Cache key · unkeyed input · Vary · Cache-Control private/no-store
Burp Param Miner · diff responses on fat headers (X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Scheme, Accept)
No edge cache for session HTML · normalize host · strip dangerous headers at edge (carefully) · explicit key recipe per route
HTTP Request Smuggling · XSS · WAF Bypass
"If the origin varies on fields the cache ignores, attackers share their response with everyone."
traps: CDNs only cache static files. -> Misconfigurations cache HTML and JSON dangerously.
Cache poisoning is the same as HTTP smuggling. -> Different mechanisms-smuggling is message framing; poisoning is key derivation vs response variance.
Vary: fixes everything. -> Over-broad Vary kills hit rates and may still miss inputs; precision matters.
Private cache-control means CDN won't store it. -> Vendors interpret directives differently-validate with tests, not assumptions.

http-request-smuggling.title: HTTP Request Smuggling
http-request-smuggling.blurb: HTTP request smuggling abuses disagreement between HTTP parsers (reverse proxy, CDN, load balancer, WAF vs origin application server) about where one request ends and the next begins.
mustKnow: Transfer-Encoding + Content-Length together on sensitive routes
CDN log differs from origin log for same request_id (if correlated)
PortSwigger Web Security Academy - Request smuggling track
CWE-444 - Inconsistent interpretation of HTTP requests
traps: Smuggling always means RCE. -> Most real-world impact is cache poisoning, session/header confusion, ACL bypass, and WAF bypass.
Duplicate Content-Length is invalid so nobody handles it badly. -> Historically, some stacks summed, picked first, or ignored duplicates-each behavior is exploitable in combination with another hop.

Transfer-Encoding: chunked is always obvious. -> Obfuscation-spacing, duplicate TE lines, identity alongside chunked, chunk extensions-tricks one parser into treating the message differently than its peer.
Disabling keep-alive fully fixes smuggling. -> It shrinks the cross-request attack surface on a single TCP connection but is costly and may not address all desync or pipeline edge cases.

http-parameter-pollution-hpp.title: HTTP Parameter Pollution (HPP)
http-parameter-pollution-hpp.blurb: HTTP Parameter Pollution arises when the same parameter name appears multiple times in a query string or body, and different components (WAF, cache, reverse proxy, application framework) parse or merge duplicates differently. Attackers abuse that split view to smuggle payloads past filters or alter server-side logic.
mustKnow: Duplicate keys → split parser behavior → filter bypass / logic bugs
First wins · last wins · concat · array - check your stack
One choke-point normalization · reject dupes on sensitive params · OpenAPI strict
Burp repeat dupes · curl -d twice · assert 400 on return_url
WAF Bypass · HTTP Request Smuggling · Open Redirect
"Same name, many values-pick one policy everywhere or reject."
traps: HPP is only a WAF problem. -> Application logic and caches also split views.
JSON can't have duplicate keys. -> Many parsers accept dupes with last-wins-still dangerous if inconsistent across services.
URL encoding fixes HPP. -> Encoding affects tokenization, not the need for a single policy.
HPP equals HTTP smuggling. -> Different mechanisms-smuggling is message framing; HPP is duplicate key merging.

http-refresh-verbs-and-status-codes.title: HTTP Refresh, verbs and status codes
http-refresh-verbs-and-status-codes.blurb: HTTP semantics (methods, safety, idempotency, status codes, and redirect behavior) shape how browsers, caches, proxies, and APIs interpret a single request.
mustKnow: 302 - historically ambiguous; many stacks treat like 303
303 - see other; GET follow-up after POST
traps: GET never changes server state. -> RFC semantics say GET should be safe, but bugs and side effects abound; defense uses authZ on every method.
302 and 303 are interchangeable. -> 303 See Other forces GET on redirect target after POST; 302 history is messier-use 303/307 intentionally.
204 means success like 200. -> 204 No Content must not include a body-clients and caches handle it differently than 200 with empty body.
401 vs 403 is pedantic. -> 401 Unauthorized (often authN missing/invalid) vs 403 Forbidden (authZ deny) guides client behavior and monitoring.

web-application-security-vulnerabilities.title: Web Application Security Vulnerabilities
web-application-security-vulnerabilities.blurb: Product security interviews expect you to move fluently between OWASP-style risk categories, concrete defenses (what you ship in code and config), and how you verify controls in production.
traps: Input validation alone prevents injection attacks -> Input validation is one layer of defense - defense in depth is required. Defense Layers for Injection: Input validation (whitelist approach preferred) Parameterized queries (SQL
HTTPS means the application is secure -> HTTPS only encrypts data in transit - it doesn't protect against application vulnerabilities.
Low-severity vulnerabilities can be ignored -> Low-severity vulnerabilities can be exploited in combination or in specific contexts to cause significant impact.

sql-injection.title: SQL Injection
sql-injection.blurb: SQL injection interferes with database queries by injecting attacker-controlled SQL fragments-often bypassing auth, exfiltrating data, or writing files depending on DB privileges. Parameterized queries / prepared statements are the primary fix; ORMs help but don't eliminate unsafe dynamic SQL.
mustKnow: ✅ Use least privilege for database users
Burp Suite: Manual testing and scanning
traps: SQL injection only affects old applications -> SQL injection vulnerabilities exist in modern applications and are still one of the top security risks (OWASP Top 10).
Only string concatenation causes SQL injection -> SQL injection can occur through multiple vectors, not just string concatenation.
Input validation prevents SQL injection -> Input validation helps but does NOT prevent SQL injection. Only parameterized queries (prepared statements) prevent SQL injection.
SQL injection only affects SELECT queries -> SQL injection affects ALL SQL operations: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and even DDL statements.

parameterized-and-prepared-statement.title: Parameterized and Prepared Statement
parameterized-and-prepared-statement.blurb: Parameterized queries and prepared statements are the primary defense against SQL injection vulnerabilities. They separate SQL code from data, ensuring that user input is always treated as data, never as executable SQL code.
mustKnow: ✅ Use parameterized queries for all user input
✅ Use prepared statements for repeated queries
traps: Prepared statements are only for performance -> Prepared statements provide both security and performance benefits. Security Benefits: ✅ Prevents SQL injection ✅ Separates code from data ✅ Database treats input as data
Input validation can replace parameterized queries -> Input validation cannot replace parameterized queries. They serve different purposes.
Prepared statements are slower for single queries -> For single queries, there may be a small overhead, but for repeated queries, prepared statements are much faster.

idor.title: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference)
idor.blurb: IDOR is a broken access control flaw: the application exposes direct references (IDs, keys, filenames) to objects and fails to verify that the authenticated user may access that specific object. It is one of the most common API and B2B findings because authorization is easy to skip on "obscure" IDs.
traps: IDOR only affects applications with sequential IDs -> IDOR vulnerabilities can occur with any type of object reference, not just sequential IDs.
Authentication prevents IDOR -> Authentication alone does NOT prevent IDOR. Authorization checks are required.
Using UUIDs instead of sequential IDs prevents IDOR -> UUIDs make enumeration harder but do NOT prevent IDOR if authorization checks are missing.
IDOR only affects REST APIs -> IDOR can occur in any application type that uses object references, not just REST APIs.

ssrf.title: SSRF
ssrf.blurb: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) is a vulnerability that allows attackers to make unauthorized requests from a vulnerable server to other internal or external resources. It ranks #10 in OWASP Top 10 2021 and is a critical web application security risk.
mustKnow: ✅ Follow redirects and validate each hop
traps: SSRF only affects HTTP/HTTPS requests -> SSRF can exploit multiple protocols and services, not just HTTP. Vulnerable Protocols: HTTP/HTTPS FTP file:// (file system access) gopher:// dict:// ldap:// Various cloud provider
WAF or firewall prevents SSRF -> WAFs and firewalls provide limited protection against SSRF. The attack originates from the server itself, which often has network access.
SSRF only affects internal networks -> SSRF can target both internal and external resources, depending on network configuration.
URL validation prevents SSRF -> URL validation is difficult and often insufficient. Many bypass techniques exist.

xxe.title: XXE
xxe.blurb: XXE abuses XML external entities so parsers resolve local files, internal URLs (SSRF), or expand entities to cause DoS. It remains relevant wherever XML is parsed with unsafe defaults-SAML, legacy APIs, SOAP, some document pipelines.
traps: XXE only affects XML parsers -> XXE can affect any application that processes XML, not just dedicated XML parsers.
Disabling external entities prevents XXE -> Disabling external entities is necessary but not always sufficient. Some attacks use internal entities or parameter entities.

XXE only allows reading local files -> XXE can lead to multiple attack vectors: Local File Disclosure (most common) Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Denial of Service (DoS) Remote Code Execution (in some cases)

JSON APIs are safe from XXE -> JSON APIs can be vulnerable if they accept XML or process XML-based formats. Vulnerable Scenarios: API accepts both JSON and XML File uploads (Office docs contain XML) SVG images

server-side-template-injection-ssti.title: Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI)
server-side-template-injection-ssti.blurb: Server-Side Template Injection occurs when user-controlled input is embedded in a template that the server evaluates as code or expression, yielding remote code execution, file read, or sandbox escapes depending on the engine. It is distinct from XSS (browser context) and client-side template issues.
mustKnow: Never concatenate user input into template source - use context variables only.
Jinja2 · Twig · Freemarker · Velocity · ERB · Razor
Static templates · sandbox + least privilege · SAST for Template( patterns · remove debug render endpoints
"User data is data, not template code-bind variables, don't compose source."
traps: Auto-escaping prevents SSTI. -> Escaping targets output encoding for HTML; SSTI is evaluation of template source.
Only PHP apps get SSTI. -> Python, Java, Ruby, .NET engines are all in scope when templates are dynamic.
Sandboxed Jinja2 is always fine. -> Misconfigurations and dangerous filters reopen surface-validate configs.
String templates are okay if input is 'validated'. -> Allow-lists rarely cover all expression metacharacters-don't build template source from users.

insecure-deserialization.title: Insecure Deserialization
insecure-deserialization.blurb: Insecure deserialization turns attacker-controlled serialized blobs into live objects in memory, enabling RCE, auth bypass, logic abuse, and data tampering via gadget chains-sequences of existing methods (gadgets) that bridge from a benign readObject (or equivalent) to dangerous behavior.
mustKnow: Untrusted bytes → object graph → gadget chains → RCE / authz break
JSON + DTO · protobuf · signed tokens · allowlist filters · patch gadget libs
SAST sinks · unexpected classes · process spawn post-request
traps: We use HTTPS, so serialized data is trusted. -> TLS protects transit-not endpoint compromise or malicious clients. Authenticate and validate payloads.
JSON is always safe. -> Type gadgets and parser bugs exist. Schema validation and safe parser settings matter.
We deserialize only our own cookies. -> Clients forge cookies-treat as untrusted unless signed and verified with strong keys.
WAF blocks deserialization attacks. -> Encoded payloads and nested structures evade signatures-fix code path.

file-upload-security.title: File Upload Security
file-upload-security.blurb: Insecure file upload lets attackers place malicious or unexpected content where the application or downstream processors (image libraries, antivirus, document parsers, ImageMagick, PDF engines) execute or mis-handle it-leading to RCE, stored XSS, SSRF, path traversal, quota abuse, and malware distribution.
traps: We only allow images, so we check the extension. -> Extensions are trivially spoofed. Use magic bytes + re-encode + allowlist.
Storing in S3 fixes everything. -> Misconfigured bucket policies (public list/get), hotlinking, and signed URL bugs still leak data.
ClamAV clean means the file is safe. -> AV misses novel polyglots and non-malware abuse (SVG XSS, zip-slip). Layer defenses.
SVG is fine if we serve it as image/svg+xml. -> Inline can still be dangerous depending on embedding and CSP. Many teams rasterize SVGs.

race-condition-vulnerabilities.title: Race Condition Vulnerabilities
race-condition-vulnerabilities.blurb: Race condition vulnerabilities arise when security or business invariants depend on ordering between concurrent operations, but the application checks a condition and acts later without an atomic guarantee.
mustKnow: Watch serialization_failure / deadlock rates after fixes.
traps: Using a database transaction automatically prevents races. -> A transaction helps only if isolation and statement patterns actually serialize conflicting access.
Race conditions only happen under huge load. -> Two well-timed requests are enough-attackers parallelize intentionally. Burp Turbo Intruder or scripts can create "load" from a laptop.
This is a threading bug, not a security issue. -> In web apps, each HTTP request may hit shared mutable state (DB rows, cache counters).
Idempotency keys are only for nice UX. -> They are a primary control for safe retries once you add serializable transactions or distributed flows.

remote-code-execution-rce.title: Remote Code Execution (RCE)
remote-code-execution-rce.blurb: Remote code execution (RCE) means an attacker can cause your system to run attacker-chosen code or system commands on a machine you control-typically the application server, worker, or container.
mustKnow: subprocess: list argv, shell=False, fixed binary path
JSON + schema instead of native binary deserialization
Patch RCE CVEs same-day class; SBOM + automation
traps: RCE always means root on the box. -> You get whatever the process user can do-often app or www-data. Container + non-root + read-only FS limits but does not make RCE "low.
WAF blocks RCE. -> WAF may catch obvious ; rm payloads; it won't stop deserialization gadgets, file-format bugs, or encrypted traffic to legit endpoints.
Only internet-facing apps matter. -> Internal services often hold more trust and weaker auth-SSRF or compromised laptop can reach them.
Severity is always Critical 10/10. -> CVSS context: scope, privileges, exploitability, data at risk. Still usually top of backlog-but communicate nuance to leadership.

graphql-and-api-security.title: GraphQL and API Security
graphql-and-api-security.blurb: GraphQL is a query language and runtime for APIs developed internally at Facebook in 2012 and open-sourced in 2015. It gives clients the power to request exactly the data they need through a single endpoint, replacing the resource-oriented URL structure of REST with a schema-driven
mustKnow: One URL, schema-driven, nested resolvers → field-level authZ and cost matter.
Introspection / schema leak Disable or gate in prod
Deep queries / aliases Depth + complexity limits, timeouts
N+1 / DB DoS DataLoader, pagination, cost analysis
Resolver SSRF No raw user URLs without allowlist
IDOR in nested types Re-check ownership per object
Per operation / cost, not only HTTP per IP.
"GraphQL isn't insecure-missing authZ and cost controls on a flexible API is."
traps: GraphQL is secure because it uses HTTPS -> TLS protects transport. GraphQL-specific risks are schema abuse, resolver logic, authZ at field level, and resource exhaustion-HTTPS does not fix those.
We can use the same WAF rules as REST -> A single endpoint and flexible queries need application-aware limits (depth/complexity, persisted queries, resolver budgets).

Introspection is fine in production for developers -> Introspection exposes attack surface to everyone who can reach the endpoint. If enabled, strong auth, network controls, or separate dev/stage endpoints are required.
Rate limiting per IP is enough -> Attackers may stay under IP limits while issuing expensive queries. You need query-aware throttles and cost controls.

grpc-and-protobuf-security.title: gRPC and Protobuf Security
grpc-and-protobuf-security.blurb: gRPC is an RPC framework that typically runs over HTTP/2 with Protocol Buffers (protobuf) as the on-the-wire message format. Security interviews expect you to separate transport trust (TLS, mTLS, mesh), application identity (tokens in metadata), authorization on every RPC
mustKnow: HTTP/2 + protobuf; often mTLS in mesh.
Metadata = headers analog; must validate per RPC.
Reflection exposes schema → usually off in prod or network-restricted.
"mTLS = trusted" - still need authZ every method.
"Protobuf = safe" - logic bugs and confused deputy remain.
Stolen client cert → attacker is a "service."
Metadata must not set identity without crypto proof.
traps: mTLS means the service is authenticated -> mTLS authenticates peers at the transport layer. You still need application-level authorization for what each RPC is allowed to do-otherwise a compromised legitimate client is
Protobuf is encrypted -> Protobuf is a serialization format. Confidentiality comes from TLS (or application encryption)-not from protobuf itself.
Reflection is harmless -> Reflection aids attackers and competitors mapping your API-treat like GraphQL introspection: environment and network controls.

websockets-and-sse-security.title: WebSockets and SSE Security
websockets-and-sse-security.blurb: WebSockets and Server-Sent Events (SSE) create long-lived HTTP-derived channels where authentication, origin policy, and per-message authorization are easy to get wrong.
mustKnow: Add rate limits, quotas, and disconnect policies.
traps: If upgrade is authenticated, every message is safe. -> Message-level authZ still matters for multi-tenant actions.
SSE is read-only so low risk. -> Data exposure and unauthorized subscriptions are still critical.
Origin checks are optional for WS. -> Missing origin validation enables cross-site abuse patterns.
Realtime channels do not need rate limits. -> Flooding and fan-out abuse can degrade service quickly.

threat-modeling.title: Threat Modeling
threat-modeling.blurb: Threat modeling is how you decide which threats deserve a control before the code hardens around the wrong assumption. You draw the system, mark where trust changes, name the threats on each crossing, and leave each one with a decision someone owns. This guide runs that session on one payment API.
mustKnow: Structured identification of threats (STRIDE, PASTA, attack trees, LINDDUN) against assets and trust boundaries, before or during design.
One change. The interfaces you can name. Checkout, the processor webhook, tenant isolation on orders. Not the marketing site. Not every action the product has.
S Spoofing AuthN, mTLS, webhook signatures
T Tampering Integrity checks, HMAC, TLS, server-side totals
R Repudiation Signed audit logs, WORM storage
I Information disclosure Encryption, least privilege, redaction
D Denial of service Rate limits, quotas, HA, idempotency keys
traps: CIA and AAA are the same thing -> CIA is a property of a thing you named. Who may read the processor token.
Design by Action and Design by Component are mutually exclusive -> They are two ways to pick where you sit. Charge-order is an action.
OTM is just another documentation format -> It is a format. Own that.
CIA only applies to data, not systems -> The processor secret in the payment pod is a confidentiality asset of the system.

system-design-for-security.title: System Design for Security
system-design-for-security.blurb: Security system design interviews ask you to architect a real product capability-login, file upload, SSO, secret rotation-under scale, latency, abuse, and compliance constraints. Strong candidates lead with abuse cases, draw trust boundaries, layer controls
mustKnow: Scope -> abuse cases -> layered controls -> failure modes -> metrics/verification
Identity · authorization · data boundaries · secrets · telemetry · response
Secure login · SSO · file upload · secret rotation · signed URLs · audit logs
Threat Modeling · IAM and Least Privilege at Scale · Secure CI CD Pipeline Security
traps: Security design is just adding WAF and MFA. -> Design quality depends on threat boundaries, authorization model, and data flow controls.
A perfect architecture can skip incident planning. -> Detection, response, and rollback paths are core design components.
Compliance architecture equals secure architecture. -> Compliance can be necessary but not sufficient for real abuse resistance.
Zero trust means zero usability. -> Risk-adaptive controls can preserve UX while reducing exposure.

zero-trust-architecture-for-product-secu.title: Zero Trust Architecture for Product Security
zero-trust-architecture-for-product-secu.blurb: Zero Trust replaces implicit trust from network location ("inside the VPN," "same VPC," "same cluster") with explicit verification of identity, device or workload trust, and authorization for every meaningful access-ideally backed by telemetry and continuous re-evaluation.
mustKnow: IdP: identities; signals: posture, risk, device health
Policy deny signal quality; incident MTTD for credential abuse
Blast radius tests / red-team findings closed
traps: Zero trust is a vendor product. -> It is an architecture and operating model (verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach)-tools implement pieces, not the whole.
VPN replacement equals zero trust. -> VPNs gate network entry; ZT emphasizes per-request policy using identity, device posture, and app context-not just tunnel shape.
Zero trust means zero network segmentation. -> Micro-segmentation and software-defined perimeters are common ZT patterns-segmentation doesn't disappear, it becomes policy-driven.
Internal traffic is trusted by default in ZT. -> East-west inspection and service identity are explicit goals-"inside" the VPC is not implicitly safe.

secure-microservices-communication.title: Secure Microservices Communication
secure-microservices-communication.blurb: This guide focuses on east-west traffic: service-to-service calls inside a platform (Kubernetes, VMs, serverless with VPC connectors). The goal is strong identity, encrypted transport, least-privilege authorization, and operable rotation-not "the private network is enough."
traps: Network isolation is sufficient for microservices security -> Network isolation is one layer - zero-trust principles require authentication and authorization for all communication.
API keys are sufficient for service-to-service authentication -> API keys are weak authentication - mutual TLS (mTLS) or JWT tokens are preferred for microservices.
All microservices should trust each other by default -> Microservices should follow zero-trust model - authenticate and authorize every request.

third-party-integration-security.title: Third-Party Integration Security
third-party-integration-security.blurb: Third-party integrations extend your product with payments, identity, communications, analytics, AI, and infrastructure services. They also move data and trust boundaries outside your direct control.
traps: Third-party security is the vendor's responsibility, not ours -> You are responsible for the security of your product, including third-party integrations.
Vendor security questionnaires are sufficient for assessment -> Security questionnaires are one component - comprehensive assessment requires multiple methods.
Third-party integrations only need to be assessed once -> Vendor security should be continuously monitored - security posture changes over time.

If a vendor is large and well-known, they're secure -> All vendors should be assessed, regardless of size or reputation. Why Size Doesn't Guarantee Security: Large vendors are attractive targets Large vendors have had security

business-logic-abuse-and-fraud-threats.title: Business Logic Abuse and Fraud Threats
business-logic-abuse-and-fraud-threats.blurb: Business logic abuse (sometimes called application abuse or workflow abuse) is the exploitation of correctly implemented features in ways that violate economic intent, policy, or fair use.
mustKnow: Valid requests, malicious intent - not only malformed input
Invariants missing: one-time use, cooldowns, idempotency, state machine gaps
Distributed attacks - single-request rules rarely enough
Broken access control / insecure design often underpin logic flaws
Software/data integrity failures matter for promo and update channels (2021 Top 10 categories) - see OWASP Top Ten for current structure
Velocity per IP / device / account / payment instrument
traps: No OWASP Top 10 finding means no fraud risk. -> Business logic abuse (coupon stacking, negative quantities, race refunds, partner API misuse) often passes scanners; it needs threat modeling and abuse cases.
Fraud is only the fraud team's problem. -> Product and AppSec own secure workflow design, rate limits, idempotency, and instrumentation before rules engines see losses.
CAPTCHA stops scripted abuse. -> Farms, solver APIs, and human click workflows adapt; layer device signals, velocity checks, and post-auth authorization.
Pen tests always find logic bugs. -> Time-boxed tests miss deep domain rules; pair with code review, property-based tests, and purple scenarios.

rate-limiting-and-abuse-prevention.title: Rate Limiting and Abuse Prevention
rate-limiting-and-abuse-prevention.blurb: Rate limiting bounds how often a client (or class of clients) may invoke an operation in a time window. Abuse prevention adds intent-aware controls: credential stuffing, scraping, payment fraud, and economic denial of service often stay below crude throughput caps if you only count HTTP requests.
mustKnow: IP First line; watch NAT/shared IPs
Algorithms: token bucket / sliding window (common at scale).
Signals: velocity, device, geo anomaly, payment risk.
Interview tip: Pair limits with observability and customer impact metrics.
traps: Rate limiting stops all bots -> Sophisticated actors stay below thresholds across many IPs/accounts. You need behavioral signals, device context, and business rules-not only request counts.

ddos-and-resilience.title: DDoS and Resilience
ddos-and-resilience.blurb: Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) exhausts network, compute, storage, or human capacity. Resilience is how you absorb, shed load, and degrade gracefully without violating safety.
mustKnow: "Attack vs viral traffic vs misconfig" - different runbooks.
"Graceful degradation" - drop non-core features under load.
Load / game-day includes authenticated worst-case paths.
Runbook distinguishes provider vs app vs cost explosion.
traps: Our autoscaler fixes DDoS -> Autoscaling can amplify cost and destabilize dependencies. You need edge controls, quotas, and financial guardrails-not only more instances.
DDoS is only volumetric -> Application-layer and economic DoS (expensive queries, account creation floods) can hurt without huge packet volume.
TLS stops DDoS -> TLS protects confidentiality/integrity of data in transit-not availability against floods of legitimate-looking TLS handshakes or L7 requests.

mobile-app-security.title: Mobile App Security
mobile-app-security.blurb: Mobile application security is the discipline of protecting iOS and Android clients and their backend APIs when the device, network, and app binary are partially hostile.
mustKnow: TLS 1.2+, strong ciphers; ATS on iOS (minimize exceptions).
Pinning: SPKI + backup pins + rotation runbook; bypassable via Frida → don't rely alone.
OAuth native: Authorization Code + PKCE (RFC 8252); no implicit flow; no client secret in app.
Prefer Universal Links / App Links over custom schemes for sensitive flows.
Validate host/path; server authZ for privileged actions.
WebView: minimal JS bridge, no OAuth, patch System WebView.
Frida/objection bypass pinning and root checks → server-side fraud + step-up.
Play Integrity / DeviceCheck as signals, not guarantees.
traps: Obfuscation equals security. -> ProGuard, DexGuard, and iXGuard raise reverse-engineering cost only. Secrets, algorithms, and authorization logic in the binary will be extracted.
Root/jailbreak detection blocks attackers. -> Checks are patchable and routinely hooked. Use integrity signals for risk scoring and step-up, not as a cryptographic guarantee.

Biometric login means the user is authenticated to the server. -> Biometrics unlock local credentials (Keychain/Keystore). Server sessions still need token issuance, expiry, revocation, and step-up for sensitive transactions.
If the UI hides the admin button, non-admins can't access admin APIs. -> Client-side authorization is not authorization. Every API must enforce roles and scopes server-side.

genai-llm-product-security.title: GenAI LLM Product Security
genai-llm-product-security.blurb: Large language model (LLM) features add a new trust boundary: untrusted natural language and documents flow through a non-deterministic model that may invoke tools, query retrieval stores, and produce outputs consumed by people and systems.
mustKnow: Tool authZ outside the model (identity, tenant, scopes, allowlists) - LLM06
Validate model output before SQL/HTML/shell/downstream APIs - LLM05
Tenant ACLs on retrieval/embeddings; cite sources; handle low-confidence - LLM08 / LLM09
Minimize + redact prompts/logs; vendor DPA/subprocessors - LLM02
Quotas + loop detection on tokens/tools - LLM10
Eval + regression after data/model changes - LLM04
"Untrusted input, high-privilege tools-authorization cannot live in the prompt."
"Indirect injection is a retrieval and UX problem, not only a chat problem."
traps: One red-team pass before launch is enough. -> Models, prompts, tools, and data change; continuous evals, regression suites, and abuse metrics are expected.
Tool-calling is safe if tools are internal. -> Over-privileged tool tokens and prompt injection can chain to SSRF, data exfil, or destructive actions-least privilege per tool.
PII in prompts is fine because the model forgets. -> Providers may log; employees review; subprocessors expand-treat prompts as sensitive telemetry.
Smaller models are inherently safer. -> Attack surface shifts but doesn't vanish-injection and abuse still apply; smaller models may hallucinate differently, not safely.

cloud-security-architecture.title: Cloud Security Architecture
cloud-security-architecture.blurb: Cloud security architecture is how you implement identity, network segmentation, data protection, logging, and resilience using cloud primitives-within the shared responsibility model.
traps: The cloud provider is responsible for all security -> Cloud security follows a shared responsibility model. The provider secures the infrastructure, but you're responsible for your data, applications, and configurations.
Encryption at rest is enough for cloud security -> Encryption at rest is necessary but not sufficient. You need defense in depth with multiple security layers.
IAM roles are more secure than IAM users -> IAM roles are generally better for service-to-service access, but both can be secure or insecure depending on implementation.
VPC isolation is enough for network security -> VPC isolation is one layer of network security, but you need additional controls like security groups, NACLs, and network segmentation.

cloud-native-security-patterns.title: Cloud-Native Security Patterns
cloud-native-security-patterns.blurb: Cloud-native applications use microservices, containers, dynamic orchestration, and API-first design-security must be platform-aligned: admission control, service identity, observability, and progressive delivery.
traps: Zero Trust means no trust at all -> Zero Trust means "never trust, always verify" - not that you don't trust anyone, but that you verify every access request.
Microservices are inherently more secure than monoliths -> Microservices can be more or less secure depending on implementation. They introduce new attack surfaces and complexity.
Serverless functions are automatically secure -> Serverless functions require explicit security configuration. Default settings may be insecure.
Cloud-native means cloud-only -> Cloud-native patterns can be applied on-premises, hybrid, or multi-cloud. It's about architecture, not location.

cloud-attack-paths.title: Cloud Attack Paths
cloud-attack-paths.blurb: Cloud attack paths are abuse chains that move from low-trust entry (stolen keys, SSRF, IMDS access, over-permissive IAM) to data exfiltration or organization-wide control. This module complements defensive Cloud Security Architecture by naming how attackers navigate AWS, Azure, and GCP control planes.
mustKnow: App bug → metadata/keys → API abuse → persist (roles, keys, Lambdas) → exfil
IMDSv1 · PassRole · AssumeRole trust chaining · public S3 · long-lived AKIA
ARM RBAC over scope · automation accounts · hybrid token theft · Key Vault policy gaps
Default SA scopes · actAs chains · exported SA keys · org policy missing
SetIamPolicy · CreateAccessKey · AssumeRole from new IP · mass GetObject
Cloud Security Architecture · SSRF · Secrets Management
"Identity is the perimeter: kill static keys, harden metadata, guardrail IAM."
traps: Private VPC means no SSRF to metadata. -> Internal SSRF from compromised workloads still reaches link-local addresses-layer controls.
MFA stops cloud privilege escalation. -> API keys and compromised workload identities bypass interactive MFA.
CSPM green means secure. -> CSPM misses app-layer authZ and insider paths-combine with pentest and CIEM.
Encryption at rest stops data theft. -> Stolen IAM creds decrypt via normal APIs-identity is king.

container-security.title: Container Security
container-security.blurb: Container security spans images, registries, runtime, orchestration (Kubernetes), and supply chain. The 4Cs (code, container, cluster, cloud) remind you that fixing only runtime misses Dockerfile, CI, and IAM.
traps: Containers are inherently secure because they're isolated -> Containers provide isolation but not complete security. They share the host kernel and can be compromised if not properly configured.
Running as root in containers is safe because it's isolated -> Running containers as root is dangerous even with isolation. Root in container = root on host if container escapes.
Image scanning is enough for container security -> Image scanning is important but not sufficient. You need runtime security, network policies, and proper configuration.
Kubernetes security is handled by the platform -> Kubernetes provides security features but you must configure and use them. Default settings are often permissive.

kubernetes-security-hardening.title: Kubernetes Security Hardening
kubernetes-security-hardening.blurb: Kubernetes security hardening is a multi‑layer discipline that spans the software supply chain, cluster control plane, admission policies, network controls, identity & access management, secrets handling, node hardening, runtime detection, and continuous verification.
mustKnow: PSA restricted · Admission policies · NetworkPolicy default-deny · RBAC least privilege · etcd encryption
automountServiceAccountToken: false · bound tokens · minimal Role
kube-bench · Kubescape · Polaris · kubectl auth can-i
Container Security · Cloud Attack Paths · PKI Program Design
traps: Kubernetes is secure by default. -> Default allows wide RBAC mistakes, no NetworkPolicy, and privileged pods unless PSA/policies applied.
Running as root in container is fine if cluster is private. -> Container escape or supply-chain RCE → root on node amplifies impact.
Service account tokens are harmless. -> Default tokens may call Kubernetes API-scope RBAC and automount: false when unused.

serverless-security.title: Serverless Security
serverless-security.blurb: Serverless security covers function-as-a-service (FaaS) and event-driven workloads-AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Google Cloud Functions, Cloudflare Workers-where you no longer patch OS images but you do own IAM roles, event trust, secrets, dependencies, and network egress.
mustKnow: One role per function (or tier: read/write/admin)
API Gateway: JWT / IAM auth, throttling, WAF
traps: Serverless means no servers, so no patching needed - we're secure. -> Provider patches the runtime; you still own code, IAM, events, secrets, and dependencies.

Environment variables are fine for API keys if the console is locked down. -> Env vars appear in CloudFormation/SAM exports, CI logs, crash dumps, and console readers with lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration.
Lambda in a VPC is automatically isolated from the internet. -> VPC attachment controls network paths, not IAM. Functions still need egress rules, NAT, and endpoint policies.
Function URLs are convenient and low risk for internal tools. -> Unauthenticated Function URLs are a common data leak vector. Require IAM auth, JWT, or front with API Gateway + WAF.

infrastructure-as-code-security.title: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Security
infrastructure-as-code-security.blurb: IaC security treats Terraform, CloudFormation, Helm, and Kubernetes manifests as code: review, test, policy-as-code, and least-privilege CI-because misconfigurations replicate at scale. Interviews focus on static scanning, drift, secrets in repos, and blast radius of CI roles.
traps: Terraform state files are safe to commit to Git -> Terraform state files contain sensitive information and should never be committed to version control.
Using variables prevents secret exposure -> Variables help but don't prevent secret exposure if secrets are stored in code, committed to Git, or passed incorrectly.
IaC security is only about preventing misconfigurations -> IaC security includes prevention, detection, response, and compliance across the entire infrastructure lifecycle.
Terraform modules are always secure -> Terraform modules can have vulnerabilities and misconfigurations. Always review and scan modules before use.

secure-ci-cd-pipeline-security.title: Secure CI CD Pipeline Security
secure-ci-cd-pipeline-security.blurb: Continuous integration and continuous delivery systems are a control plane: they read source code, execute arbitrary build steps, hold credentials, and often gate production releases.
mustKnow: OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks - v1.0 stable October 2022; cites SolarWinds, Codecov, dependency confusion, and compromised packages in intro.
Flow control - 2. IAM - 3. Dependency chain - 4. Poisoned pipeline execution - 5. PBAC - 6. Credential hygiene - 7. Misconfiguration - 8. Third-party services - 9.
SEC-1/4 Branch protection, required reviews, protect workflow files
SEC-2/5 Least-privilege CI identities; scoped cloud roles
SEC-6 OIDC to cloud; short-lived tokens; no long-lived keys in CI
SEC-8 Pin actions/plugins (commit SHA); allowlist vendors
SEC-9 Sign artifacts; verify at deploy; digest pin images
traps: SAST/DAST green means the pipeline is secure. -> Pipeline identity, runner trust, secret handling, artifact signing, and deployment gates are orthogonal to app scanning.
Self-hosted runners are always safer than cloud runners. -> Poorly patched pets with broad network egress and shared workspaces increase blast radius vs ephemeral cloud builders.
One broken gate means we should bypass forever. -> Bypass needs time-bound approval, ticket, and remediation SLA-permanent exceptions become norm.
Fork PRs can't steal secrets. -> Misconfigured workflow triggers and cache poisoning patterns have leaked credentials-restrict GHA permissions and use OIDC.

software-supply-chain-security.title: Software Supply Chain Security
software-supply-chain-security.blurb: Software supply chain security is the discipline of keeping what you build, buy, and run faithful to intended source, build, and distribution: from a developer's laptop and third‑party dependencies through CI/CD, artifacts, registries, and runtime.
mustKnow: Lockfiles + pins + digests for prod artifacts
Private registries / approved upstreams where possible
SBOM per release artifact + owner + SLA
SLSA-style provenance where feasible; verify at deploy
Triage: EPSS/exploit intel + reachability + tier-not CVSS-only
Incident playbook for malicious package or compromised pipeline
"SBOM answers what; SLSA/provenance answers how; deploy verification answers whether we run it."
traps: Only open‑source dependencies are risky. -> Build plugins, container base images, internal packages, CI templates, SaaS integrations, vendor binaries, and IDE extensions are all common compromise paths.
Signing once in CI is enough. -> Verification must happen where artifacts are consumed: at the registry on push, at the deployment gate, and at runtime policy enforcement.

SLSA level on paper equals SLSA in practice. -> Process and tooling must match the claim; auditors and red teams care about forged metadata, weak build isolation, and provenance that isn't actually verified.
Dependabot / Renovate fixes supply chain risk. -> They reduce known CVE exposure, but they don't fix malicious packages, typosquatting

secure-source-code-review.title: Secure Source Code Review
secure-source-code-review.blurb: Secure code review means reading source with an attacker's eye so vulnerabilities and design flaws get caught before release. In practice you combine three things: tooling (SAST, dependency scanners), a working catalogue of bug classes
traps: Automated SAST tools can replace manual code review -> Automated SAST tools and manual code review are complementary - both are essential for comprehensive security assessment.
Input validation alone prevents injection attacks -> Input validation is one layer of defense - defense in depth with parameterized queries and output encoding is required.
Cryptographic libraries are always secure by default -> Cryptographic libraries must be used correctly - misconfiguration or improper usage can create vulnerabilities.
Client-side validation is sufficient for security -> Client-side validation is for user experience only - security must always be enforced server-side.

product-security-assessment-design.title: Product Security Assessment Design
product-security-assessment-design.blurb: Product security assessments evaluate how a feature or product behaves under realistic abuse, not only whether a scanner found a CVE. This guide is written for security engineers who must scope work, model threats at feature granularity, collect defensible evidence, communicate to engineering and product
traps: Security assessments should test everything equally -> Security assessments should be risk-based, focusing on high-risk areas first. Risk-Based Approach: Identify critical assets and data Prioritize high-risk attack vectors Focus on
Automated tools are sufficient for security assessments -> Automated tools are valuable but insufficient - manual testing and expert analysis are essential.
Security assessments are one-time activities -> Security assessments should be continuous and iterative, not one-time checkboxes.

Finding all vulnerabilities is the goal of security assessments -> The goal is risk reduction, not finding every possible vulnerability. Risk-Based Goals: Identify critical and high-severity issues Understand overall security posture Provide

penetration-testing-and-security-assessm.title: Penetration Testing and Security Assessment
penetration-testing-and-security-assessm.blurb: This guide frames how penetration testing, vulnerability scanning, and crowdsourced testing differ; how to run engagements safely under clear rules of engagement; how to report in a way engineering and leadership can act on; how to validate remediation; how purple-team exercises fit the picture
traps: Penetration testing and security assessment are the same thing -> Penetration testing is a subset of security assessment - they serve different purposes.

Automated tools can replace manual penetration testing -> Automated tools and manual testing are complementary - both are needed. Automated Tools: Good for finding known vulnerabilities Efficient for large-scale scanning Consistent
Penetration testing should test everything with equal intensity -> Penetration testing should be risk-based, focusing on critical assets and high-risk areas.

Finding all vulnerabilities is the goal of penetration testing -> The goal is risk reduction, not finding every possible vulnerability. Realistic Goals: Identify exploitable vulnerabilities Understand attack surface and risk Provide actionable

proactive-security-assessment.title: Proactive Security Assessment
proactive-security-assessment.blurb: Proactive security assessment means finding and fixing security weaknesses before they become incidents-by embedding lightweight reviews, threat modeling, and measurable controls into how product and engineering teams already work.
mustKnow: "We'll make it as easy as possible"
"Security is here to help, not block"
traps: Security assessments slow down development and should be avoided -> Well-integrated security assessments can accelerate development by catching issues early when they're cheaper and faster to fix.
Security assessments are only needed before production release -> Security assessments should be continuous throughout the development lifecycle, not just at the end.
Only security team can perform security assessments -> Security assessments are a shared responsibility - security team enables, developers participate.
Security assessments always require external consultants -> Many security assessments can be done internally with proper tools and processes.

rapid-security-triage-fast-checking.title: Rapid Security Triage (Fast Checking)
rapid-security-triage-fast-checking.blurb: Rapid security triage is the discipline of taking an inbound signal-scanner finding, researcher report, pen-test note, bug-bounty submission, or engineer's "is this bad?"-and quickly deciding validity, severity, owner, and next action without drowning in false positives.
traps: Highest CVSS always goes first. -> Unreachable dead code, disabled features, or strong compensating controls can lower effective risk.
Fast triage means skip reproduction. -> Fast means tiered repro-one curl for reflected XSS vs deep chain for RCE. Never zero evidence for P0.
Triage is junior work. -> Wrong calls burn millions (wasted eng time or missed breach). Senior triage is judgment under uncertainty.
We can close duplicates without linking. -> Duplicate without reference reopens and wastes reporter trust. Always link canonical ticket.

security-bug-identification-and-validati.title: Security Bug Identification and Validation
security-bug-identification-and-validati.blurb: Security bug identification and validation is the end-to-end craft of finding suspected weaknesses (code review, testing, reports) and proving whether they are real, exploitable, and worth fixing-with clear reproduction steps, impact analysis, and responsible handling.
mustKnow: Report → repro → impact → dedupe → severity → route → verify fix
Build/version · role · steps · HTTP/logs · minimal case · no secrets in ticket
Self-XSS · unreachable dep CVE · default mitigation already on · intended behavior
Exploitability · exposure · data · integrity · KEV/EPSS (CVE class)
Rapid Triage · Vuln Management · Code Review · Pen Testing
"Repro first, evidence packaged, impact in context, dedupe, verify closure."
traps: No repro means no bug. -> Some issues (crypto design) need analysis not PoC-still require written argument.
Validation is someone else's job after I file. -> Quality in = quality out-incomplete reports waste cycles.
Duplicate reports are spam. -> Duplicates signal confusing UX or docs-merge and improve guidance.
Exploit code is required for acceptance. -> Clear logical proof often suffices; weaponized PoC may be restricted by policy.

waf-bypass-and-defense-evaluation.title: WAF Bypass and Defense Evaluation
waf-bypass-and-defense-evaluation.blurb: A Web Application Firewall (WAF) inspects HTTP(S) requests (and sometimes responses) against signatures, heuristics, and ML models before traffic reaches the application.
mustKnow: Edge inspection → (optional TLS terminate) → origin (authoritative security)
Encoding nest · parser diff (JSON/XML) · HPP · multipart tricks · smuggling-adjacent normalization · path variants
Baseline attacks · mutation matrix · FP on prod-like traffic · log proof · latency / error budget
Fix app → strict edge normalization → tuned virtual patch → schema/mTLS for APIs → monitor canaries
Burp · nuclei · ModSecurity/CRS · cloud WAF logs (AWS/CF/Akamai patterns)
HTTP Request Smuggling · HTTP Parameter Pollution · SSRF
"Treat WAF as parser differential territory: measure FN/FP on your routes, fix the app, use WAF as depth."
traps: If the WAF blocks sqlmap, we're safe. -> Custom encodings, nested parsers, and alternate API paths often evade signature sets.
ML WAFs can't be bypassed. -> Adaptive attackers probe blind spots; ML also drifts with traffic shifts.
We can skip code fixes because virtual patch exists. -> Virtual patches rot, fail-open, or get disabled when noisy. Root-cause fix is durable.
Blocking is always better than logging. -> Aggressive block can DoS legitimate clients; tuning needs FP budget and observability.

fuzzing-security-testing.title: Fuzzing Security Testing
fuzzing-security-testing.blurb: Fuzzing (fuzz testing) feeds semi-random or mutated inputs to a program to trigger crashes, hangs, or logic violations. For security, the goal is to find memory corruption, assertion failures, parser bugs, and unexpected states before attackers do.
mustKnow: Mutate inputs → execute under instrumentation → keep interesting cases → triage crashes
Dumb random · Mutation + corpus · Coverage-guided (AFL++, libFuzzer) · Grammar / generation
Narrow API · reset state · timeouts · good seeds · dictionary (optional)
AFL++ · libFuzzer · Honggfuzz · cargo fuzz · ClusterFuzz pattern
Fuzzing Methodology and Campaign Design · Crash Analysis · Secure Code Review
"Coverage-guided fuzzing + sanitizers finds memory and parser bugs early; triaged like any security defect."
traps: Fuzzing guarantees no bugs remain. -> Fuzzing explores stochastically; logic bugs, race conditions, and crypto issues often need other methods.
We can fuzz production APIs directly. -> Unauthorized load is illegal / out of scope; fuzz staging or isolated services with approval.
No crash means secure. -> Silent wrong behavior without a crash (pure logic flaws) may not be caught by crash-only oracles.
libFuzzer is only for C++. -> Clang toolchain supports C; other languages use FFI harnesses or language-specific fuzzers.

fuzzing-methodology-and-campaign-design.title: Fuzzing Methodology and Campaign Design
fuzzing-methodology-and-campaign-design.blurb: Fuzzing methodology is how you turn ad-hoc fuzzer runs into a repeatable security program: choosing targets, building harnesses and corpora, running with sanitizers, measuring coverage, triaging crashes into actionable bugs, and closing the loop with fixes and regression seeds.
mustKnow: inventory → prioritize → harness + seeds → run (+sanitizer) → dedup/triage → fix → regression seeds
Network exposure · user-controlled formats · privilege · historical bug density · harness cost
Opaque binary Coverage-guided mutation + rich seeds
New edges/week · unique security bugs · MTTR for crashers · job uptime · open S0/S1
Owner per target · SLA · dashboards · no silent risk accept without named accountability
libFuzzer · AFL++ · honggfuzz · ClusterFuzz / OSS-Fuzz patterns · llvm-cov
traps: Raw crash count is our KPI. -> Unique defects fixed, coverage growth, and regression prevention outperform duplicate crash totals.
We can fuzz production traffic captures as seeds. -> PII and contractual constraints often forbid this. Prefer scrubbed or synthetic corpora.
No crashes means we can stop fuzzing. -> New code, compiler changes, and config drift reopen surface. Campaigns should be continuous or regression-gated in CI.
Grammar fuzzers are set-and-forget. -> Specs evolve. Stale grammars miss new branches; they need versioning like production parsers.

osint-for-security-assessments.title: OSINT for Security Assessments
osint-for-security-assessments.blurb: Open-source intelligence (OSINT) for security assessments is the lawful, policy-aligned collection of public (or client-authorized) information to map attack surface, people, technology, and third parties-before or during penetration tests, red teams, threat intelligence, and due diligence.
mustKnow: Lawful, scoped collection of public (or authorized) data to support security assessments-not exploitation by itself.
DNS · CT logs · ASN/RDAP · search dorks · code repos · Wayback · job posts · app stores
CT, DNS enum via API Port scan, httpx probes
Seeds → subdomain enum → resolve → correlate tech → prioritize → document sources
Dedicated browser/VM · rate limits · minimal PII · approved tools
traps: OSINT is always legal. -> Collection method, jurisdiction, target, and use matter. Active probing, credential stuffing, or bypassing ToS can be illegal or breach contract.
More data is always better. -> PII sprawl increases GDPR/privacy risk and hurts report quality. Targeted collection wins.
Personal social media is off limits. -> Public posts may be fair game ethically for high-level context, but many employers restrict targeting individuals-follow RoE.
GitHub secrets are the client's fault only. -> Report responsibly; coordinate rotation; avoid public disclosure without agreement.

osint-methodology-and-operational-safety.title: OSINT Methodology and Operational Safety
osint-methodology-and-operational-safety.blurb: This module covers how to run OSINT safely and repeatably: methodology (plan → collect → analyze → report), operational security for researchers, privacy and legal constraints, and coordination with stakeholders. It pairs with OSINT for Security Assessments (sources and workflow) and emphasizes safety first.
mustKnow: Objective → scope → collect (passive) → analyze → report → dispose
Dedicated profile/VM · rate limits · no personal blur · encrypted notes · approved tools
RoE first · minimize PII · cite sources + time · corroborate · escalate legal gray zones
Credential stuffing · port scanning · exploitation · bypassing auth
OSINT for Security Assessments · Initial Access · Penetration Testing
"Plan, scope, collect passively, document provenance, protect yourself and subjects with legal + OPSEC hygiene."
traps: OSINT is anonymous and consequence-free. -> Logs, ToS, and law apply; clients can audit your actions.
Public data can be used any way we want. -> GDPR and other laws limit processing even of public personal data.
Scraping is always passive OSINT. -> Automated requests can be active and legally risky-scope it.
Personal social targeting is fine for pentests. -> Harassment and non-consensual surveillance cross ethical and legal lines-define boundaries in RoE.

initial-access-and-attack-surface-entry.title: Initial Access and Attack Surface Entry
initial-access-and-attack-surface-entry.blurb: Initial access is the first adversary foothold inside a target environment (MITRE TA0001). Attack surface entry is the set of externally reachable interfaces-email, web, remote services, identity flows, supply chain, people-that can yield that foothold.
mustKnow: TA0001 Initial Access - foothold before lateral movement
Phish · valid accounts · edge RCE · supply chain · trusted relationship
Shrink surface · phishing-resistant MFA · CA/device posture · fast edge patch · segmentation
Auth anomalies · email threat · perimeter telemetry · first-run endpoint behaviors
Threat Modeling · Supply Chain · SSRF · Advanced Red Team Operations
"Inventory externals, kill anonymous admin, harden identity, patch edge, segment, detect early."
traps: Initial access always means 0-day. -> Credentials and unpatched known CVEs dominate real incidents.
Supply chain risk is just npm typosquatting. -> Build systems, signing keys, vendor updates, and CI secrets are in scope.
Blocking countries stops initial access. -> Geo blocks are noisy and bypassed via residential proxies; identity and app security matter more.
Detection can replace prevention here. -> High signal prevention (no admin on internet, MFA) reduces detection load and blast radius.

basic-exploitation-fundamentals.title: Basic Exploitation Fundamentals
basic-exploitation-fundamentals.blurb: Basic exploitation connects a vulnerability (memory corruption, logic bug) to attacker-chosen behavior using primitives like control of instruction pointer, arbitrary read/write, or script execution.
mustKnow: Bug → primitive → compose → goal (exec / leak / bypass)
Stack overflow · UAF · type confusion (adjacent topic)
Exploit Development · Shellcode Fundamentals · Windows Exploit Mitigations
"Primitives compose under mitigations; patch beats gadget hunting."
traps: Every crash is exploitable. -> Many are DoS only; triage proves control and reachability.
Stack smashing still means shellcode on stack. -> DEP breaks executable stack models for most modern OSes.
Heap is just like stack but slower. -> Different invariants; exploit techniques differ.
Mitigations are a substitute for fixes. -> Mitigations reduce probability; bugs still need patches.

exploit-development.title: Exploit Development
exploit-development.blurb: Exploit development is the disciplined process of turning a vulnerability primitive (e.g., memory corruption, unsafe deserialization) into a reliable capability-often arbitrary code execution or controlled data flow-under specific environment constraints.
mustKnow: Stack overflow · heap corr · UAF · double free · type confusion
ROP - reuse gadgets for NX bypass (high level)
Safe languages · sandbox · fuzz + fix · fast patch · least privilege
Authorized labs only · no unsanctioned targets
traps: Every crash is RCE. -> Many crashes are NULL derefs or asserts with no control. Triage determines exploitability.
ASLR means we're safe from memory bugs. -> ASLR is one layer; info leaks, partial overwrites, and logic bugs still defeat it.
Exploit dev is only for attackers. -> Defenders use exploitability analysis for patch priority, bug bounty triaging, and sandbox design.
Mitigations are bulletproof. -> Bypass research continues; assume breach and layer controls.

exploit-development-learning-path.title: Exploit Development Learning Path
exploit-development-learning-path.blurb: This module is a structured study path from crash triage to mitigation-aware exploit reasoning-not a weaponization course. It connects C memory models, debuggers, fuzzing, ROP basics, and modern mitigations so you can discuss offensive and defensive tradeoffs in interviews ethically.
mustKnow: C/asm → debugger fluency → triage → mitigations → platform track → professional ethics
Linux CTF density · Windows enterprise mitigations + WinDbg
Explain overflow + DEP · minimize crash · map bug to CWE · no rogue targets
gdb/lldb · WinDbg · pwntools · sanitizers · optional angr
Exploit Development · Basic Exploitation Fundamentals · Windows Exploit Mitigations · Shellcode Fundamentals and Detection
"Foundations, authorized labs, mitigation-aware reasoning-depth matches role, ethics always."
traps: Exploit dev == only shellcode. -> Heap, JIT, logic, kernel, and browser chains dominate modern research.
Windows is 'harder,' so skip it. -> Enterprise AppSec interviews still expect WinDbg-level literacy at senior tiers sometimes.
Offense knowledge means you can't do defense. -> Strong defenders often understand offense within ethical bounds.

crash-analysis-for-security.title: Crash Analysis for Security
crash-analysis-for-security.blurb: Crash analysis for security is the process of triaging reproducible faults-from fuzzers, sanitizers, production crashes, or bug reports-to decide exploitability, severity, root cause, and fix priority.
mustKnow: Repro → minimize → root cause → security impact → dedupe → route
OOB read/write · UAF · double free · stack smash · null deref
ASan/UBSan · gdb/lldb bt · WinDbg !analyze · symbolicated mobile stacks
User control? Primitive strength? Reachable? Mitigations?
Stack signature + component + fault class - verify same fix
creduce · rr · symbol servers · issue tracker automation
Fuzzing · Exploit Development · Rapid Triage · Vuln Management
"Repro reliably, minimize, read the sanitizer, assess control, dedupe, severity with evidence."
traps: If ASan says heap overflow, it's always exploitable. -> Sanitizer finds undefined behavior; exploitability needs control and reachability analysis.
All crashes from fuzzing are security bugs. -> OOM, timeouts, and logic asserts may be quality only-classify before CVE.
Stack trace alone is enough to close as duplicate. -> Different inputs can hit same frame via different paths-verify root cause.
Production crashes are too noisy to use. -> Sampling + symbolication + clustering surfaces real regressions-especially after releases.

shellcode-fundamentals-and-detection.title: Shellcode Fundamentals and Detection
shellcode-fundamentals-and-detection.blurb: Shellcode is position-independent machine code injected or staged to extend an initial memory-corruption primitive into arbitrary behavior (spawn shell, load PE, callback). Detection spans static signatures, emulation, memory permission anomalies (RWX), ETW/EDR telemetry, and CPU features (Intel CET, ACG).
mustKnow: PIC · stager/stageless · badchars · ROP under DEP
RWX / unexpected RX · alloc→write→protect→thread · unbacked memory · ETW/EDR API telemetry
DEP · ASLR · CFG/ACG · CET · fix the vuln
YARA · memory scanners · Sysmon · debuggers for triage
Exploit Development · Windows Exploit Mitigations · EDR Evasion Awareness
"Shellcode is small machine code after a primitive; detect memory + behavior, harden with mitigations, patch the bug."
traps: Shellcode always touches disk. -> Many chains are fileless-memory-only injection is common.
RWX pages are always malware. -> Some JIT runtimes legitimately use RW→RX transitions; context and module provenance matter (FP risk).
DEP alone stops shellcode. -> ROP to VirtualProtect / NtProtectVirtualMemory is a classic evasion of W^X assumptions.
Kernel shellcode is the same as user shellcode. -> Privilege, calling conventions, and exploit constraints differ; detection surfaces differ (PatchGuard, HVCI context).

windows-security-boundaries.title: Windows Security Boundaries
windows-security-boundaries.blurb: Security boundaries on Windows separate trust levels: kernel vs user, session isolation, integrity levels (UIL), AppContainer sandboxes, and virtualization-based security (VBS) features like HVCI.
mustKnow: Kernel ↔ user · Session · Integrity level · AppContainer · VBS (HVCI, Credential Guard)
Token privileges · ACLs · WDAC/AppLocker · hypervisor-backed CI
UAC ≠ strong boundary · Patch privesc · segment tier 0
Windows Exploit Mitigations · EDR Evasion Awareness and Defense
"Policy lines on objects and tokens-VBS hardens kernel trust; assume user code is hostile."
traps: UAC stops malware. -> UAC prompts aren't a kernel boundary; user malware remains dangerous.
Antivirus equals kernel protection. -> Kernel drivers and BYOVD can undermine AV; defense is layered.
Credential Guard blocks all PtH. -> Reduces many classes; misconfigurations and alternate paths remain.
Admin password rotation fixes escalation. -> Token theft and persistence don't care about password age alone.

windows-exploit-mitigations.title: Windows Exploit Mitigations
windows-exploit-mitigations.blurb: Windows exploit mitigations are compiler, loader, and kernel features that raise the cost of turning memory corruption into reliable code execution: DEP (NX), ASLR, stack canaries, CFG (Control Flow Guard), ACG (Arbitrary Code Guard), CET (Shadow Stack / IBT), and heap hardening.
mustKnow: DEP/NX · ASLR · /GS canary · CFG · ACG (context) · CET (shadow stack / IBT)
Exec data · predictable bases · trivial stack smash · unrestricted indirect calls · some returns
Basic Exploitation Fundamentals · Windows Security Boundaries · EDR Evasion Awareness
"Layered compiler and OS controls raise exploit cost-patch still wins."
traps: CFG stops all ROP. -> CFG narrows targets; research continues on valid call sites and data-only attacks.
DEP is obsolete. -> Still foundational; attackers adapt with ROP, JIT spray less common on modern browsers but primitives evolve.
64-bit ASLR is always high entropy. -> Images without DYNAMICBASE, fork without rebase, and leaks reduce entropy.
Kernel and user mitigations are identical. -> Kernel has PatchGuard, HVCI, different exploit constraints.

keylogger-architecture-and-detection.title: Keylogger Architecture and Detection
keylogger-architecture-and-detection.blurb: A keylogger captures keystrokes (or clipboard, IME, auto-fill) to steal credentials and secrets. Architectures span user-mode hooks (SetWindowsHookEx, raw input), polling screens/accessibility APIs, kernel filter drivers, hardware implants, and browser extensions.
mustKnow: User hooks · UIA/screen · kernel filter · hardware · browser ext
Hook DLLs · injection · new drivers · Sysmon Image loads · extension policy
HVCI/driver policy · EDR · strong MFA · physical controls
EDR Evasion Awareness · Windows Security Boundaries
"Input pipeline interception-layer driver policy, hook visibility, and identity resilience."
traps: Antivirus always catches keyloggers. -> Signed or fileless variants evade static scans.
Kernel loggers are extinct. -> Abused where drivers can load; policy matters.
HTTPS stops keyloggers. -> TLS protects network; keyloggers read before encryption.
Screen keyboards are always safe. -> OSK can still be scraped or clicked by malware with access; raises bar, not absolute.

edr-evasion-awareness-and-defense.title: EDR Evasion Awareness and Defense
edr-evasion-awareness-and-defense.blurb: Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) collects process, file, registry, network, and kernel telemetry to detect and investigate threats. Evasion techniques attempt to blind user-mode hooks, abuse signed drivers (BYOVD), spoof process trees, or blend with legitimate admin activity.
mustKnow: User hooks · ETW · kernel callbacks · network off-box
Unhook · direct/indirect syscalls · BYOVD · PPID spoof · LOLBins
HVCI · WDAC drivers · sensor tamper protection · kernel visibility · assume gaps
ntdll integrity · new drivers · impossible parent edges · rare CLI chains
Windows Security Boundaries · Shellcode Fundamentals and Detection
"Hooks lie; layer kernel policy, driver control, and behavior hunts."
traps: BYOVD is theoretical. -> Abused in real intrusions; driver policy matters.
If malware is signed, it's safe. -> Stolen certs and repurposed tools break that assumption.
Studying evasion is only for attackers. -> Defenders must understand blind spots to engineer detections.

active-directory-attacks.title: Active Directory Attacks
active-directory-attacks.blurb: Active Directory (AD) is the identity and authorization backbone of most enterprise Windows estates. Offensive interviews expect you to connect Kerberos and NTLM mechanics to named abuse patterns (Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, NTLM relay, DCSync
mustKnow: DCs · krbtgt · AD CS CA · AADC servers · Tier 0 workstations (should be zero)
AS-REP roast · Kerberoast · DCSync · NTLM relay · Pass-the-Hash · Golden/Silver tickets · AD CS template abuse
gMSA for SPNs · kill pre-auth exceptions · SMB/LDAP signing · EPA · tier model · CA template audit
4769 Kerberos service ticket · 4662 DS access · Cert enrollment events
Windows Security Boundaries · MITRE ATTACK Interview Fluency
"Kerberos secrets + ACL edges + PKI mistakes = domain compromise-graph it, tier it, sign it."
traps: Azure AD means on-prem AD doesn't matter. -> Hybrid connect syncs identities; on-prem compromise propagates cloud risk.
Disabling Kerberos fixes everything. -> NTLM fallback and legacy apps widen relay surface-migrate safely, don't toggle blindly.
BloodHound is only offensive. -> Defenders use the same graph to find over-permissioned paths before attackers.
