Pentest found no DA-AD is clean. -> Time-boxed tests miss ACL depth; continuous assessment tools find latent edges.

advanced-red-team-operations.title: Advanced Red Team Operations
advanced-red-team-operations.blurb: Advanced red team operations are goal-oriented adversary simulations that test people, process, and technology against realistic threat actors-with explicit authorization, rules of engagement, and measurable learning outcomes.
mustKnow: Objectives · Threat profile · RoE · Safety · Metrics · Reporting · Remediation owners
TTD · TTC · ATT&CK coverage · detection rule hit rate · replay after fix
Beaconing · LOLBins · lateral movement · identity abuse
traps: Red team findings are always Critical. -> Chained Mediums can be worse than single Critical CVE. Narrative risk matters.
Offensive tools in prod are fine with a letter. -> RoE must cover each action; mistakes can still be criminal or contract breach-operational discipline required.
ATT&CK mapping is bureaucracy. -> It enables coverage metrics and communication with blue team-use technique level appropriately.

mitre-attack-for-security-interviews.title: MITRE ATT&CK (Interview Fluency)
mitre-attack-for-security-interviews.blurb: MITRE ATT&CK® is a knowledge base of adversary tactics (the why) and techniques (the how), organized by platform (Enterprise, Mobile, Cloud, ICS). Interviewers use it to test whether you can map controls and detections to real behaviors, not recite matrix colors.
mustKnow: Recon → Resource Dev → Initial Access → Execution → Persistence → Priv Esc → Defense Evasion → Credential Access → Discovery → Lateral Movement → Collection → C2 → Exfil
Cite techniques you know; avoid guessing IDs.
Navigator layers · detection prioritization · purple atomic tests · CTI mapping
traps: ATT&CK is only for SOC analysts. -> Architects, AppSec, and CTI all use it for shared vocabulary.
Full matrix coverage is the goal. -> Prioritize techniques matching your adversaries and architecture-breadth without depth wastes time.
Cloud matrix is identical to Enterprise. -> Different techniques and scopes-use the right matrix.
If a technique isn't listed, it's not a risk. -> ATT&CK is living and not exhaustive-novel behaviors exist.

cve-walk-throughs.title: CVE Walk-Throughs
cve-walk-throughs.blurb: CVE walk-throughs are how senior interviewers test whether you understand real incidents beyond headlines: the root cause, exploitation primitive, blast radius, detection signals, patch/compensating controls, and organizational lessons.
mustKnow: Context → Root cause → Primitive → Chain → Detection → Remediation → Lessons
Log4Shell Log4j JNDI in logs → RCE
Heartbleed TLS heartbeat overread → rotate keys
Citrix Bleed Token memory leak → session hijack
traps: Knowing CVE names equals depth. -> Interview depth is mechanism + mitigation reasoning, not name recall.
CVSS alone is enough for priority. -> Exposure and active exploitation evidence often dominate urgency.
Only RCE CVEs matter. -> Auth bypass and data disclosure flaws can be equally business-critical.
Public PoC means immediate compromise. -> Reachability and environment controls still matter.

production-security-incident-response.title: Production Security Incident Response
production-security-incident-response.blurb: This guide describes how product and platform security teams respond when something goes wrong in live production: from the first credible signal through containment, eradication, recovery, customer impact, forensic logging, communications, legal obligations, and post-incident improvement.
mustKnow: Contain first, fix root cause later
traps: The first priority in an incident is to fix the vulnerability -> The first priority is to contain the incident and prevent further damage, not to fix the root cause.
Taking systems offline is always the best containment strategy -> System shutdown is a last resort - use least-disruptive containment methods first.
Incident response can be improvised when needed -> Incident response requires preparation and practice - you can't improvise under pressure.
Security incidents should be kept secret from stakeholders -> Transparency and communication are critical, though communication should be controlled and appropriate.

multi-team-security-incident-response.title: Multi-Team Security Incident Response
multi-team-security-incident-response.blurb: Security incidents in production rarely stay inside one team. Customer impact, regulatory clocks, evidence preservation, and public trust all depend on how SRE, security, legal, communications, product, and executives work together under time pressure.
mustKnow: ✅ Separate channels for technical vs. business
traps: Incident response coordination can be figured out during the incident -> Incident response requires preparation and practice - roles and procedures must be defined beforehand.
One person should make all decisions during incidents -> Incident response benefits from structured decision-making with clear authority and escalation paths.
Communication should wait until all facts are known -> Regular communication is critical, even with incomplete information - silence creates uncertainty.

security-observability-and-detection-eng.title: Security Observability and Detection Engineering
security-observability-and-detection-eng.blurb: Security observability is the practice of making security-relevant behavior visible, attributable, and measurable across infrastructure and applications. Detection engineering turns that visibility into testable hypotheses expressed as rules, queries, and models, with explicit ownership, tuning, and retirement.
mustKnow: Generate telemetry → normalize (ECS/OTel) → retain by tier → detect (rules/ML) → respond (SOAR/runbooks) → learn (postmortems → new content)
actor.user.id · src.ip / http.request_id · process.executable · cloud.region · auth.mfa bool · normalized outcome (allow/deny)
Crown-jewel paths (admin, money, data export, secret read)
Identity abuse (impossible travel, new device, OAuth consent spam)
Host persistence and lateral movement primitives
App-layer abuse (rate spikes, coupon abuse signals)
traps: More logs means better security. -> Unstructured volume drowns analysts; taxonomy, retention tiers, and parsing quality determine value.
SIEM go-live equals detection maturity. -> Maturity is measured by coverage of attack paths, tuning cycles, and purple validation-not ingestion TB/day.
We can buy detections out of the box. -> Vendor rules need environment baselines, allow-lists, and correlation with identity context-tuning is mandatory.
Detection engineering is just writing Sigma rules. -> Data model design, on-call runbooks, metrics, false negative postmortems, and stakeholder communication are core work.

vulnerability-management-lifecycle.title: Vulnerability Management Lifecycle
vulnerability-management-lifecycle.blurb: Vulnerability management (VM) is the disciplined loop from discovery through triage, prioritization, remediation, verification, and measurement. It spans code, dependencies, hosts, containers, cloud control planes, and third-party services.
mustKnow: CVSS - technical severity vector; environmental metrics adjust for your network
EPSS - probability of exploitation in the wild (continuously updated)
KEV (CISA) - known exploited vulns → patch now discipline for US-adjacent orgs
traps: CVSS 10 means drop everything -> CVSS is a useful input but not business impact. A CVSS 10 on an internal admin-only system may differ from a 7 on an Internet-facing auth path-context matters.
Scanning equals vulnerability management -> Scanning produces candidates. Value comes from triage, ownership, SLAs, and verified fixes-otherwise it's noise.
We can fix everything immediately -> Capacity is finite-prioritization and risk acceptance with expiry are part of mature programs.

risk-prioritization-and-security-metrics.title: Risk Prioritization and Security Metrics
risk-prioritization-and-security-metrics.blurb: Risk prioritization is how security teams turn findings into decisions: what to fix first, what to accept with compensating controls, and what to measure so the program actually improves.
mustKnow: CISA KEV - known exploited CVEs (KEV catalog)
Mean time to remediate criticals / KEV items
Control coverage (signed artifacts, MFA, JIT, etc.)
traps: More closed tickets means lower risk. -> Volume can improve while crown-jewel exposures or unfixed 0-days remain untracked.
Executive dashboards should show every finding. -> Leadership needs decision-grade top risks, trend, and capacity tradeoffs-not raw scanner exports.
We should optimize for mean time to patch everything. -> Uniform SLAs waste capacity; tier assets and align SLAs to blast radius.
Security scorecards are objective. -> Weighting choices embed values; publish methodology and avoid gaming via narrow definitions.

security-metrics-and-okrs.title: Security Metrics and OKRs
security-metrics-and-okrs.blurb: Security metrics make risk and program health legible to engineering, product, and the board. OKRs (Objectives and Key Results) translate that visibility into quarterly outcomes without rewarding the wrong behavior-such as inflating severity, closing tickets cosmetically
mustKnow: MTTR for sev-1 security issues Compare severity consistently
% criticals past SLA Don't hide in "won't fix"
Control coverage in CI Activity ≠ effectiveness
Repeat incident classes ↓ Needs root-cause discipline
Refs: FIRST (CSIRT practices); FAIR/CVSS used with judgment.
Cross-read: Risk Prioritization and Security Metrics (detailed), Vulnerability Management Lifecycle.
traps: More findings means better security -> High signal findings can rise when detection improves-it's not automatically bad.
OKRs should be 100% secure -> OKRs should be measurable and achievable with trade-offs acknowledged-residual risk is normal; document it.

building-an-appsec-program.title: Building an AppSec Program
building-an-appsec-program.blurb: Building an AppSec program answers the interview scenario: "You're the first security hire at a 200-person startup-what do you do in the first 90 days?" Success requires charter, asset inventory, risk-based prioritization, developer partnerships, tooling with low noise
mustKnow: 60d Risk tiers, CI baseline, champions, threat models
90d Pilot gate, pen test, metrics, roadmap
Design reviews · Consult SLAs · Champion sync · Monthly metrics
Secure SDLC Walkthrough · False Positive Management · Risk Prioritization
traps: Compliance is the program. -> Compliance is one input; exploitability and business risk drive priorities.
Developers are the enemy. -> Partnership model wins; punitive gates fail at scale.

secure-sdlc-walkthrough.title: Secure SDLC Walkthrough
secure-sdlc-walkthrough.blurb: The Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) maps security activities to each phase of delivery-requirements → design → implementation → verification → release → operations-so security is built in, not bolted on before launch.
mustKnow: Requirements Data class, abuse cases, compliance NFRs
Design Threat model, arch review, third-party risk
Build Standards, SAST/SCA/secrets in CI, PR review
Test DAST, authZ tests, pen test/bounty
Release IAM/config review, SBOM, canary metrics
Operate Vuln SLAs, IR feedback, metrics
DoD security items · Sprint-0 arch review · CI gates · Exception workflow
traps: Security is a phase before release. -> Shift-left means continuous activities; a single pre-release scan is too late for design flaws.
Threat modeling is only for big projects. -> Small features can introduce critical authZ bugs-scope modeling by risk, not headcount.
Developers don't do security. -> AppSec enables developers with standards, tools, and champions-they write the code.
Compliance equals secure SDLC. -> SOC 2 checkboxes without effective gates still produce vulns.

agile-security-compliance.title: Agile Security Compliance
agile-security-compliance.blurb: Agile teams optimize for small batches, fast feedback, and changing priorities. Compliance programs (especially SOC 2 and ISO 27001) optimize for demonstrable, repeatable controls and evidence. The failure mode is treating compliance as a release gate or audit-week scramble.
traps: Compliance is only needed at release, not during development -> Compliance should be continuous throughout SDLC, not just checked at release. Continuous Compliance: Security checks in development (code scanning) Compliance checks in CI/CD

Compliance requirements are fixed and can't adapt to Agile -> Compliance can be adapted to Agile while maintaining security objectives. Agile Compliance Approaches: Risk-based compliance (focus on high-risk areas) Continuous compliance

Compliance means 100% security -> Compliance ensures baseline security but doesn't guarantee complete security. Compliance vs. Security: Compliance: Meeting regulatory/standard requirements Security: Actual

security-development-collaboration.title: Security-Development Collaboration
security-development-collaboration.blurb: Product security succeeds when engineering ships secure software at sustainable pace. Collaboration is not a soft skill layered on top of technical work
mustKnow: Product security succeeds when engineering ships secure software at sustainable pace.
traps: Security team's role is to block insecure code -> Security team's role is to enable secure development, not to gatekeep or block. Enablement Approach: Provide tools and frameworks Offer guidance and training Participate in design

Security reviews should happen at the end of development -> Security should be integrated throughout SDLC, not added at the end. Shift-Left Security: Security in design phase (threat modeling) Security in development (secure coding
Security issues are always high priority and must be fixed immediately -> Security issues should be prioritized based on risk, not treated as all equally urgent.

Security training is a one-time event -> Security awareness and training should be ongoing and contextual. Continuous Learning: Initial security training for new developers Regular security updates and workshops

security-vs-usability-balance.title: Security vs Usability Balance
security-vs-usability-balance.blurb: This guide is for product security and engineering leaders who must ship controls users will actually follow. The goal is not to "pick security or usability," but to align assurance, friction, and clarity so the secure path is the path of least resistance.
mustKnow: Security and usability can be complementary
Measure and iterate on security UX
traps: Security and usability are always in conflict -> Security and usability can be complementary - good security design enhances usability.
Maximum security always requires maximum friction -> Risk-based approaches can reduce friction while maintaining appropriate security.
Users will always choose convenience over security -> Users will choose convenience if security is too burdensome - make security easy and transparent.
Security features that reduce usability should be removed -> Some security friction is necessary - focus on minimizing unnecessary friction while maintaining security.

false-positive-management.title: False Positive Management and Tool Rationalization
false-positive-management.blurb: False positive management is how AppSec teams keep SAST, DAST, SCA, and cloud scanners usable: without tuning, engineers ignore findings, disable rules, or lose trust in security gates.
mustKnow: Diff-based gates · Rule tuning · Path excludes · Reachability · Baseline
CVE + component + path · CWE + file + line
One primary per question: secrets · SCA · SAST · DAST · CSPM
Signal ratio · Time to triage · Suppression expiry backlog
"Tune for signal, not score-developers must trust the gate."
traps: Zero false positives is the goal. -> Goal is actionable signal; some FP cost is OK if triage is fast and gates are diff-based.
Developers should triage all SAST findings. -> AppSec/champions tune rules; devs fix confirmed issues-don't dump raw scanner output.

product-security-real-world-scenarios.title: Product Security Real-World Scenarios
product-security-real-world-scenarios.blurb: This guide collects scenario-style prompts-design reviews, incident judgment, trade-offs, and stakeholder conflicts-typical of product security interviews. Use scenarios to practice structured answers: clarify constraints, name threats, propose controls, verify, and measure-not encyclopedic trivia.
